items.evidence: Recursion is when a function calls itself to solve a smaller version of the same problem.
items.note: The student clearly defined recursion as a function calling itself.

items.evidence: Every recursive function needs a base case, which is the condition where it stops calling itself...
items.note: The student stated that a recursive function requires a base case.
The student explained that the base case returns a result without making further recursive calls.

items.evidence: The recursive step has to change the argument, like n minus 1, so each call gets closer to the base case.
items.note: The student explained that each recursive call operates on a smaller subproblem.

items.evidence: Each call is pushed as a new stack frame on the call stack, holding its own parameters and local variables.
items.note: The student explained that independent stack frames are pushed onto the call stack.

items.evidence: If there is no base case, or it is never reached, the frames keep piling up until the stack runs out of space and the program crashes with a stack overflow.
items.note: The student stated that an absent or unreachable base case triggers a stack overflow.
The student did not mention that any recursive algorithm can be rewritten iteratively.
The student did not explain tail call optimization.

target_reason: This is an important foundational concept about the equivalence of recursion and iteration.
target_focus: how to do the same thing using loops instead of calling itself
